captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 6. In this lesson: Plastic in the ocean.
Read an argument and identify points, evidence and linking words.
Here are some new words. Pollution. Damage to air, water or land caused by harmful things. Single-use.
Made to be used only once and then thrown away. Marine. To do with the sea.
And some more words. Reduce. Make smaller or less. Harmful. Causing damage. Alternative.
Another thing you can choose instead.
Time for a question. The video will stop.
Which word means: damage to air, water or land caused by harmful things?
Now some grammar: Linking words for arguments.
Use firstly, furthermore, in addition, however, therefore and in conclusion to organise an argument.
For example: Firstly, plastic harms sea animals. For example: However, some plastic is useful.
For example: Therefore, we should use less.
Now listen, and read along. Why we should ban single-use plastic at school.
Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic end up in the ocean.
Our school should stop using single-use plastic, and here is why.
Firstly, plastic is harmful to marine life.
Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and eat them. Furthermore, plastic does not disappear.
A plastic bottle can take around 450 years to break down.
However, some people say that plastic is cheap and convenient.
This is true, but there are good alternatives, such as metal water bottles and paper straws.
Therefore, I believe our school should ban single-use plastic by next year.
In conclusion, small changes at school can help to reduce pollution in the whole ocean.
Another question. The video will stop. What does the writer want the school to do?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like pollution, single-use, marine.
You practised linking words for arguments. And you read Why we should ban single-use plastic at school.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 6. In this lesson: A formal letter.
Write politely and formally, and use have to and don't have to.
Here are some new words. Formal. Serious and polite, used in official writing. Request.
Ask politely for something. Recycling bins. Containers for things that can be used again.
And some more words. Consider. Think carefully about something. Sincerely.
A polite way to end a formal letter. Suggestion. An idea you offer for someone to think about.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: serious and polite, used in official writing?
Now some grammar: have to and don't have to. ‘Have to’ means something is necessary.
‘Don't have to’ means it is not necessary, so you can choose. For example: Students have to wear a uniform.
For example: You don't have to bring lunch – the school provides it.
Now listen, and read along. A letter to the head teacher. Dear Mrs Okafor,
I am writing on behalf of the Year 6 Eco Club to request more recycling bins for our school.
At the moment, there is only one recycling bin, which is next to the office. As a result,
most students have to walk a long way to recycle,
so many simply throw paper and bottles into the ordinary bins.
We would like to suggest placing a recycling bin in every classroom.
The Eco Club is happy to empty them every Friday, so the cleaners would not have to do any extra work.
We hope that you will consider our suggestion. Thank you for your time.
Yours sincerely, Daniel Mensah, Eco Club leader.
Another question. The video will stop. Who is the letter to?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like formal, request, recycling bins.
You practised have to and don't have to. And you read A letter to the head teacher.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!
